strong.text: Your chart is the strong kind, {dm_short}, so add one more layer to the story above. Strong charts remember a relationship as a series of positions they held. You can probably recite your case: what you asked for, what they failed to do, the night it became obvious. Most of it may even be accurate. What a strong chart files away is how much room was left for the other person to be right about anything. Try this once, on paper. Write the three complaints they would make about you, in their words, at their most reasonable. Not the cruel version, the fair one. If you can't think of three, that's the finding. If you can, you now hold the half of the story you were missing, and you can stop arguing with someone who isn't in the room.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Write their three fair complaints about you. Their version, not your rebuttal.

weak.text: Your chart is the weak kind, {dm_short}, which shapes how you tell this story. A weak chart tends to take the whole bill. You may have already decided it ended because you were too much, or not enough, or both at once, depending on the hour. That feels like honesty. It is closer to habit. Try sorting it into three piles: what was yours, what was theirs, and what belonged to the timing, the city, the job, the season of life you were both in. Most breakups split across all three. If your first pile is enormous and the other two are empty, you are not being accurate, you are being polite to someone who is gone. Give the other piles their fair share. It doesn't excuse anything you did. It just puts the weight where it actually sits.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Three piles: yours, theirs, and the timing. You don't get to carry all of them.

strong.text: With a strong chart, the pattern above usually runs on willpower. You decide how you are going to handle this, and then you handle it, often visibly. The gym, the new project, the perfectly normal posts. People tell you that you seem fine, and you take it as proof. The catch is that a strong chart can outrun a feeling for months without ever digesting it. It turns up later as irritation at a stranger who reminds you of them, or a sudden flat week you can't explain. You don't need to slow down your whole life. You need one place where the plan stops. A friend with permission to ask how you actually are, or ten minutes at night where you write what you felt today rather than what you did. Strength that never sets anything down gets heavy.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Fine is not a feeling. It's a press release. Who gets the real version?

weak.text: With a weak chart, the pattern above tends to run on other people. You lean on friends, you replay the conversation for anyone who will listen, and you take their opinions in until you are not sure which one is yours. You also absorb the ex's version of events more than you should, because a weak chart doubts its own read first. None of this is a flaw. Support is exactly what a weak chart needs. The adjustment is about choosing it. Pick two people whose judgment you trust and stop polling the rest. Mute the group chat that turns your breakup into a series. And keep one small daily thing that is entirely yours, a walk with the same route, a page in a notebook, a song you play only for yourself. Recovery for you is less about time and more about getting your own voice back.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Pick two people whose advice you trust. Thank everyone else and stop the poll.

strong.text: For a strong chart the pull often has a competitive edge, and it is worth naming. Part of you is not only missing them. Part of you wants the last word, the proof that you were the better loss, the version of events where they realize it. That is why checking can feel like research rather than longing. Look at what you are looking for when you open their profile. Are you hoping they are sad, or hoping they are fine so you can stop worrying, or checking whether someone new has appeared? Each answer means something different. The strong-chart fix is a rule you set once and keep, since you are good at keeping rules: no checking on weeknights, or no checking at all for thirty days. You don't need more willpower for this. You need to point the willpower you already have at the right target.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Wanting to win the breakup is still being in it. Pick a different contest.

weak.text: For a weak chart the pull is usually about reassurance. Checking their stories gives you a tiny hit of contact, a sense that the connection still exists somewhere, even one way. The trouble is that every check also reopens the question of whether you were enough, and a weak chart answers that question harshly at night. Notice the time of day you reach for your phone. It is rarely random. Tired, alone, slightly hungry, end of a long day: the moments your support is lowest are the moments the pull is loudest. So the fix is less about discipline and more about logistics. Put something else in that slot. A call with someone who likes you, a show you are halfway through, the phone charging in the kitchen. You are not weak for wanting comfort. You just deserve comfort that doesn't cost you the next morning.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Notice when the pull hits. Tired and alone? Put a kinder thing in that slot.

strong.text: Here is the strong-chart part of the honest answer. If a second chance ever came up, the question wouldn't be whether you could make it work. You can make a lot of things work by effort. The question is whether you would let it be different. A strong chart tends to restart a relationship from the same position it left, with better arguments. Before you spend more energy on the question of them, spend some on this list: what you would want to change in yourself, what you would need them to change, and which of those you could check without asking anyone. If the list is all their changes, you have your answer about the timing, at least from your side.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: If your plan for round two is 'same me, better arguments,' rethink round two.

weak.text: Here is the weak-chart part of the honest answer. When support is thin, a person who once made you feel steady can start to look like the only source of it. That makes the question of whether they come back feel enormous, as if your whole footing depends on it. It doesn't, even though it feels that way at 1am. Before you weigh what you want, ask what you are actually missing: the person, or the sense of being held. If it is the second, some of that can be rebuilt with friends, routines and rest, and you will think much more clearly about the first once you have.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Are you missing them, or missing feeling held? Both are real. Only one needs them.

strong.text: A note for strong charts on that first reply: your instinct may be to take control of the conversation. Set the terms, deliver the summary, ask the pointed question. It feels like self-respect. To the other person it can feel like walking into a meeting. If you ever get a message, let the first reply be short and warm and leave room for them to say why they wrote. You can be clear later. A useful line: "Good to hear from you. What made you reach out?" Then really wait to hear it. You lose nothing by listening first, and you learn far more than you would by talking.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Short and warm first. You can be clear in the second message.

weak.text: A note for weak charts on that first reply: your instinct may be to say yes to whatever they offer, a coffee, a call, a vague let's see, because any contact feels better than none. Slow that down. Wait a few hours before you answer anything, and write your reply somewhere other than the chat box first. Read it back and ask whether it says what you want or only what keeps them talking. A useful line: "I'm glad you wrote. I need a day to think about how I want to answer." That sentence protects you without closing anything. People who matter can wait a day.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Draft it in your notes app, not the chat box. Thumbs are not decision makers.

strong.text: One more thing for a strong chart: give the energy a job. You have more drive than you know what to do with right now, and unused drive turns into rumination. Pick one project with a finish line inside the next six weeks. A course, a room you repaint, a race you train for, a shelf of books you finally read. Something with visible progress. It is the classic remedy for a strong Day Master, letting the excess flow out into work you can see, and it beats arguing with a memory. While you do it, practice one soft skill on purpose: ask a friend how they are, then ask a second question before you talk about yourself.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Give your drive a project with a finish line. Your ex is not a project.

weak.text: One more thing for a weak chart: rebuild your supports before you test them. That means sleep before strategy, food before big talks, and people who know you well before people who are new. Weak charts recover by being fed, which in saju terms means getting more of what nourishes you rather than pushing harder. Make a short list of what refills you, and treat it like medicine you take daily, not a treat you earn. Keep your commitments small for a few weeks and say no without explaining. You don't owe anyone a busy, impressive recovery. A quiet one counts.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Sleep, food, your people. Strategy can wait until you're fed.

peer_strong.text: Your chart is heavy on {dm_el}, the same element as your Day Master. In saju that is the peer family, the energy of siblings, rivals and your own reflection. A lot of it means you are self-reliant to a fault. In a relationship that shows up as two people negotiating rather than one couple deciding, because you were never fully willing to hand over the steering wheel. It can also make you competitive with the person you love: who apologized more, who sacrificed more, who is coping better now. The upside is resilience. Charts like yours rarely stay knocked down. The work is learning that needing someone does not cancel your independence. You can stand on your own and still ask to be met halfway.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Your chart is basically a room full of you. Nobody else could get a word in.

output_strong.text: Your chart is heavy on {heavy_el}, the element your {dm_el} produces. Saju calls this the output family: talent, expression, words, the things you make. With a strong Day Master behind it, output is a gift that can also run your mouth. You probably said a lot in this relationship, and said it well. You may also have said the sharp version, the clever version, the one you couldn't take back. Output also rebels against rules, so a partner who tried to manage you would have met resistance on principle. Right now that energy wants to explain the breakup to everyone, publish the playlist, write the long message. Let it make something instead. A song, a letter you never send, a sketchbook. The expression is real. It just shouldn't be aimed at them.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Heavy {heavy_el} means you're good with words. Also good at sending them at midnight.

wealth_strong.text: Your chart is heavy on {heavy_el}, the element your {dm_el} controls. Saju calls this the wealth family, and it is less about money than about what you reach for and manage: plans, outcomes, the shape of a shared life. A strong Day Master can carry a lot of it, so you are probably the one who organized things. The trips, the lease, the five-year idea. In love that can tip into treating the relationship as a project you were running, and when it ended it may feel like a failed project as much as a lost person. Notice that. A person is not a result. If you want to understand what happened, ask where you were managing instead of meeting them, and where you were steering a story they hadn't agreed to.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: You held the plans together. That was love too. It just wasn't the whole of it.

power_strong.text: Your chart is heavy on {heavy_el}, the element that controls your {dm_el}. Saju calls this the power family: rules, duty, pressure, the boss and the referee. A strong Day Master can handle it, which makes you disciplined and serious about commitments. You meant what you promised. The shadow is that you may have held the relationship to a standard, and yourself to an even higher one, until it felt more like a test than a home. After a breakup, power energy becomes a judge. It asks what you did wrong, then what they did wrong, then whether you are allowed to feel this bad. Loosen the courtroom. Some things ended because two decent people wanted different lives, and no ruling is required.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Your inner referee wants a verdict. Some breakups end in a draw. This may be one.

resource_strong.text: Your chart is heavy on {heavy_el}, the element that feeds your {dm_el}. Saju calls this the resource family: care, learning, protection, the mother element. On a strong chart there is plenty of it, which makes you thoughtful, comfortable with your own company and slow to panic. It also makes you a deep thinker who can think a feeling to death. You may have spent this breakup researching attachment styles and rereading old messages for clues, cushioned in analysis, without doing much. Resource energy prefers understanding to action. The move is small and physical: one decision you act on this week. Return their things, archive the chat, book the haircut. Understanding is lovely, but you already have plenty of it.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: You've understood this breakup from every angle. Now do one small thing about it.

output_weak.text: Your chart leans on {heavy_el}, the element your {dm_el} produces. That is the output family: expression, effort, giving. On a weak chart it drains more than it refills, a little like a phone running too many apps on low battery. In love you likely gave a lot, in words, favors, time, attention, and the giving felt natural until you noticed you were tired all the time. The breakup may hurt partly because you poured so much out and have little left to process it with. Your remedy is to stop producing for a while. No long explanations, no posts, no making sure everyone else is okay with how it ended. Let people bring you things for once.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: You poured out so much. Let the tank refill before you explain anything to anyone.

wealth_weak.text: Your chart leans on {heavy_el}, the element your {dm_el} controls. That is the wealth family: what you reach for, manage and try to hold. Classical readers have a phrase for this setup, wealth heavy and self light. There is a lot you want to carry, and not much behind you to carry it with. In love that can look like taking responsibility for the whole relationship, its moods, its plans, its survival, while quietly running on empty. If it ended, part of the hurt may be relief you feel guilty about. Let that be okay. Your job right now is not to rescue anything. It is to put down what was never yours alone to hold.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: You tried to carry the whole relationship on one arm. That's not loyalty. It's a sprain.

power_weak.text: Your chart leans on {heavy_el}, the element that controls your {dm_el}. That is the power family: pressure, rules, other people's expectations. On a weak chart it lands hard, the classic picture of heavy pressure on a light frame. You may have spent the relationship trying to be acceptable, checking your tone, smoothing things before they happened. After a breakup that pressure turns into a voice that sounds like a disappointed teacher. It is loud, and it is not a fact. Your remedy is the element that feeds you, the opposite of pressure: rest, kindness, people who don't grade you. Lower the bar this month, on purpose. You'll think more clearly without the whistle.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: That strict voice in your head isn't the truth. It's just loud. Lower the volume.

rooted_on_paper.text: Here is what that means for this breakup. You may look steady from the outside, the one with opinions and a plan, and still feel shaky underneath, because the support in your chart is scattered rather than rooted. That gap is why you can sound sure about the relationship in the afternoon and doubt everything by midnight. Neither mood is lying. One is the plenty you see, the other is the root you don't have. Treat the midnight version gently and don't make decisions there. Make them at noon, after food, ideally after talking to someone who knows you.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Confident at noon, doubting at midnight. Make your decisions at noon.

output_strong.text: {miss_el} is missing from your visible chart, and for your {dm_el} it is the output element, the channel feelings leave through. A strong chart without an outlet is a pressure cooker. You probably didn't say the important things in the relationship, or said them only once things boiled over. That pattern matters more than any single fight. You can borrow output on purpose: say one true sentence a day to someone safe, write instead of rehearse, move your body until something loosens. Expression is a skill, and you can learn it like any other.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: No {miss_el} means no outlet. You don't vent. You erupt. Schedule smaller vents.

wealth_strong.text: {miss_el} is missing from your visible chart, and for your {dm_el} it is the wealth element, the part of life you aim at and shape. A strong chart without a target can circle. You have plenty of energy and not always a clear place to put it, so a relationship can become the place, and its end leaves a lot of force with nowhere to go. Borrow the missing element by picking concrete targets: one thing you'll finish, one thing you'll fix, one thing you'll build. Give your strength something solid to hold that isn't a person.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Spare energy needs a target. A shelf to build beats a person to fix.

power_strong.text: {miss_el} is missing from your visible chart, and for your {dm_el} it is the power element, the referee. A strong chart with no referee writes its own rules and changes them when it likes. That is freedom, and it can also mean you didn't notice when you crossed a line, or when a line of theirs mattered more than you thought. Borrow structure from outside: a friend who is allowed to call you out, a few promises to yourself you keep in writing. Boundaries from outside feel strange at first. Then they start to feel like respect.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: No referee in your chart. That's why 'I didn't think it was a big deal' keeps happening.

resource_strong.text: {miss_el} is missing from your visible chart, and for your {dm_el} it is the resource element, the one that cares for you and teaches you to rest. You are strong without it, which usually means you learned to look after yourself early. The cost is that receiving care feels awkward. You may have been easier to love than to comfort. During a breakup that turns into a stubborn I'm fine. Borrow the missing element: let someone cook for you, take the advice you'd give a friend, sleep in without earning it.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Let someone bring you soup. You don't have to earn it first.

output_weak.text: {miss_el} is missing from your visible chart, and for your {dm_el} it is the output element, how feelings get out. On a weak chart that is partly protective. You don't leak energy into every conversation, which helps when your reserves are low. The downside is that hurt gets stored rather than spoken, and stored hurt tends to show up later as tiredness. You don't need a big outlet. Small ones work better: a voice note to a friend, two lines in a journal, a song you sing badly in the car. A little release, often.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Hurt you never say still finds a way out. Let it out in small, gentle doses.

wealth_weak.text: {miss_el} is missing from your visible chart, and for your {dm_el} it is the wealth element, the urge to grab hold of results. On a weak chart, that absence can be a quiet blessing. You are less likely to chase, and more likely to wait and see. The risk is the other direction: drifting, letting things happen to you, including the ending. Borrow a little wealth energy in tiny, concrete doses. One clear wish, said out loud. One small thing you decide rather than accept. Practice choosing on low stakes first.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Start with lunch. Choose it yourself. Work up to bigger choices.

power_weak.text: {miss_el} is missing from your visible chart, and for your {dm_el} it is the power element, outside pressure and rules. For a weak chart that is mostly good news: one fewer thing pressing on you. It can also mean you never learned to ask for structure, so you either had none or borrowed your partner's, and now theirs is gone. Build a light version of your own. A bedtime, one standing plan per week, a rule about late-night texting. Structure you choose isn't pressure. It's a handrail.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: No pressure element. Good. Now pick one gentle rule and let it hold you up.

resource_weak.text: {miss_el} is missing from your visible chart, and for your {dm_el} it is the resource element, the one that feeds you directly. That helps explain why support matters so much to you, and why losing someone who felt like home can knock you flat. It isn't a flaw in you. Your chart simply doesn't come with its own supply. So you build it from outside, on purpose: people who are kind to you, rest you don't apologize for, learning something new that belongs only to you. Collect sources. One person was never supposed to be all of them.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Comfort works better from five places than from one. Start collecting.

none_strong.text: Every one of the five elements turns up somewhere in your pillars, even if some only as hidden stems. On a strong chart that gives you range. You can be blunt and tender, practical and dreamy, and you have probably been all of those in this relationship. The risk with range is choosing whichever mode wins the argument in the moment. When you think about them now, notice which mode is talking. Fight-mode makes it look one way, missing-them mode another. Neither one is the whole picture.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: You've got all five elements. Including one that just wants to win the argument.

none_weak.text: Every one of the five elements turns up somewhere in your pillars, even if some only as hidden stems. On a weak chart that means you have more tools than you think. What you lack is root, not range. You can comfort, plan, speak, finish and rest. You just tire faster, so you need to pick which one the day calls for instead of trying all five. Today, maybe that's rest. Tomorrow, maybe that's a conversation you've been putting off. One element at a time is plenty.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: You have all five tools. You don't have to use them all on the same day.

resource.title: What steadies you: {helper_el}
resource.text: Every chart has an element that brings it back to balance. For a weak {dm_el} chart it is the one that nourishes your Day Master, and for you {helper_el}, your resource element. In a breakup this is the most practical thing in your whole reading. When you feel scattered, you don't need more insight about them. You need more {helper_el} in your days. Think of it as feeding the root instead of trimming the branches. When the root is fed, the questions about them get quieter on their own, and your judgment about what you want comes back.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Your steadying element is {helper_el}. Less insight about them, more of that.

peer.title: What steadies you: {helper_el}, your own element
peer.text: Every chart has an element that brings it back to balance. Yours already has plenty of the element that feeds you, so what helps most is your own, {helper_el}. That means people who are like you, friends who were here before the relationship and will be here after it, and activities that remind you who you are without anyone's input. A weak chart that already has plenty of nourishment on paper doesn't need more advice or more comfort. It needs company that stands next to it, people who are on your level and on your side.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Your steadying element is your own, {helper_el}. Go back to the people who knew you first.

output.title: What balances you: {helper_el}
output.text: Every chart has an element that brings it back to balance. A strong {dm_el} chart doesn't need more support. It needs a way to let the strength out, and for you that is {helper_el}, the element your Day Master produces. The breakup advice that fits you is not rest and reflection. It is expression and motion. Use the energy instead of sitting on it. Sitting still with a strong chart tends to turn into replaying, and replaying turns into a story you keep telling yourself. Moving, making and finishing things lets the same force come out as something you can be proud of a month from now.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Your balancing element is {helper_el}. Translation: stop stewing and start doing.

wealth.title: What balances you: {helper_el}
wealth.text: Every chart has an element that brings it back to balance. Yours is strong and already pours a lot out, so what helps most is {helper_el}, the element your Day Master works on and shapes. In plain terms, you need concrete targets. Tasks with edges. Things you can finish and point at. A breakup leaves a lot of loose energy, and you settle best when it has somewhere solid to go. A list with three items you can tick off by Friday will calm you more than a long talk about feelings, at least at first. The talk can come later, once the energy has somewhere to land.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Your balancing element is {helper_el}. Give your energy something with edges.

wood.text: {helper_el} in real life looks like growth and green things. Walks under trees, a new skill with a beginner's level, plants on the windowsill, plans that point forward. It is the element of starting, so start something small that isn't about them.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Wood looks like walks, plants and starting something new. Go green for a while.

fire.text: {helper_el} in real life looks like warmth and people. Sunlight in the morning, dinners with friends who make you laugh, saying the thing out loud instead of thinking it, music loud enough to feel. It is the element of visibility, so let yourself be seen by people who are glad to see you.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Fire looks like sunlight, laughter and saying it out loud. Go where it's warm.

earth.text: {helper_el} in real life looks like routine and home. Regular meals, the same bedtime, cooking something slow, a walk on the same route, friends you can sit with in silence. It is the element of the center, so keep your days simple and predictable for a while.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Earth looks like regular meals, early nights and a calm home. Boring is medicine.

metal.text: {helper_el} in real life looks like edges and order. Clearing a drawer, archiving the chat, a clean desk, a firm no, finishing things. It is the element of the harvest, cutting what is done so the rest can breathe. Tidy one physical space and notice how much quieter your head gets.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Metal means edges. Archive the chat, clear the drawer, finish the thing.

water.text: {helper_el} in real life looks like rest and depth. Long sleep, baths, swims, quiet evenings, reading, journaling, conversations that go slow. It is the element of winter, when things restore underground, so give yourself permission to look less productive and recover more.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Water looks like sleep, slow evenings and quiet. Recovery counts as doing something.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Rat spouse palace. Did they ever meet the real you, or just the clever one?

ox.text: Saju reads the branch sitting under your Day Master as the spouse palace, the private room a partner lives in. Yours holds the Ox, 丑, cold wet Earth that stores Metal and Water. In love the Ox is loyal, patient and slow to let go, which is exactly why breakups take you longer than your friends expect. You don't switch off. You carry the field until you're sure it's fallow. That loyalty is a virtue. It also means you may still be keeping promises to a relationship that has released you from them. Write down one promise you're still keeping, and decide whether you want to.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Ox spouse palace: still keeping old promises. You're allowed to set them down.

tiger.text: Saju reads the branch sitting under your Day Master as the spouse palace, the private room a partner lives in. When things end, the Tiger's reflex is to leap somewhere new, a city, a job, a person. Sometimes that's healthy. Sometimes it's running with style. Before your next big leap, sit still long enough to name what you're leaping away from.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Tiger spouse palace: you leap away from pain. Sit for a minute first.

rabbit.text: Saju reads the branch sitting under your Day Master as the spouse palace, the private room a partner lives in. In the next relationship, say the small disagreement while it's still small. Peace that is kept by silence tends to end suddenly.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Rabbit spouse palace: you kept the peace. Next time, keep the truth too.

That's why the loss can feel larger to you than the relationship looked from outside. You're grieving the stored future too. Name it, on paper. Then decide which parts of that future you could still build without them.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Dragon spouse palace: you're grieving a future they never saw. Name it.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Snake spouse palace: you look finished with it. Let one person see the rest.

horse.text: Saju reads the branch sitting under your Day Master as the spouse palace, the private room a partner lives in. Yours holds the Horse, 午, midsummer Fire and one of the peach-blossom branches. Up close you're passionate, honest and allergic to feeling penned in. Breakups hit you fast and loud, and you move fast and loud afterward too. That speed protects you and also skips steps. Before you gallop into the next thing, walk a lap. What did this relationship give you that you'd want again? What did it cost that you won't pay twice?

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Horse spouse palace: walk one lap before the next gallop.

goat.text: Saju reads the branch sitting under your Day Master as the spouse palace, the private room a partner lives in. Yours holds the Goat, 未, warm late-summer Earth that stores Wood. Up close you're tender, artistic and a quiet worrier, the one who looked after the mood of the relationship. After a breakup the Goat worries about the other person's feelings almost as much as its own. That's kind, and it can delay your own grief. Give your worry a new address for a while: you.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Goat spouse palace: you're worrying about their feelings. Worry about yours.

monkey.text: Saju reads the branch sitting under your Day Master as the spouse palace, the private room a partner lives in. Yours holds the Monkey, 申, early-autumn Metal with Water inside, and one of the travel branches. Up close you're quick, funny and restless, and you probably got through the worst days of this breakup with jokes. Humor is a real strength. It is also a door you close on the feeling. Let one conversation about the breakup stay unfunny from start to finish. You'll be surprised how much lighter you feel afterward.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Monkey spouse palace: great breakup jokes. Now have one unfunny conversation.

rooster.text: Saju reads the branch sitting under your Day Master as the spouse palace, the private room a partner lives in. Yours holds the Rooster, 酉, pure autumn Metal and one of the peach-blossom branches. Up close you're precise, honest and exacting, and you have a sharp eye for what went wrong. After a breakup the Rooster can turn that eye on itself and pick every flaw. Use the precision kindly. Name one thing you'd do differently, specifically, and one thing you did well, just as specifically. Both lists deserve the same attention to detail.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Rooster spouse palace: list what you did well, with the same precision.

dog.text: Saju reads the branch sitting under your Day Master as the spouse palace, the private room a partner lives in. Yours holds the Dog, 戌, dry autumn Earth that stores Fire. Up close you're loyal and protective, slow to trust and fierce once you do. That's why betrayal, or anything that felt like it, cuts so deep. You may still be standing guard over the relationship, defending it to friends or defending yourself against it. You can stop patrolling. Loyalty is meant for people who are here, starting with you.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Dog spouse palace: you're still guarding a house nobody lives in. Come home.

pig.text: Saju reads the branch sitting under your Day Master as the spouse palace, the private room a partner lives in. Yours holds the Pig, 亥, early-winter Water with Wood inside, and one of the travel branches. Up close you're warm, trusting and generous, quick to forgive and quick to hope. After a breakup that generosity can keep you rewriting the story so your ex comes out well. Kind, but not always accurate. Let the story include the times you were let down too. Seeing them clearly doesn't make you less kind.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Pig spouse palace: you keep forgiving the story. Let it be accurate too.

me_strong.text: You ended it. With a strong chart that usually means you decided, and once you decide, you defend the decision. Some days that feels like clarity. Other days, especially when you see them looking fine, it can flip into doubt, and a strong chart hates doubt, so it argues back. Two things can be true at once: it was the right call, and you still miss them. Missing someone is not a sign you chose wrong. It is a sign the relationship had real good in it. Stop asking the decision to prove itself every week. It already did its job.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: You ended it and you still miss them. Both true. Stop re-trying the case.

me_weak.text: You ended it. With a weak chart that took more courage than people realize, because ending things means disappointing someone, and you are wired to avoid that. Since then you may have carried guilt like a second bag. You might even have softened the ending so much that they aren't sure it happened. Check that. Kindness is not the same as vagueness, and a clear ending is gentler on you both than a door left half open. You are allowed to have made a hard choice and to feel sad about it without taking it back.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Hard choice, real sadness. Neither one means you should undo it.

them_strong.text: They ended it. For a strong chart that lands as two hurts at once: the loss, and the loss of control. You may find yourself drafting arguments, rebuttals, the message that will make them see it clearly. That message rarely changes anything, because their decision wasn't a debate you lost. Let it be their decision, even if you think it was wrong. You can disagree with it completely and still respect that it belonged to them. Your energy is better spent on the part you do control: how you want to come out of this, and who you want to be when you think about it a year from now.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: No rebuttal changes a decision that was never up for a vote.

them_weak.text: They ended it. For a weak chart that tends to land as a verdict on your worth, and it isn't one. A breakup is information about what someone could or couldn't do in that relationship at that time. It is not a score. You might be replaying moments to find the one where you lost them. That search usually ends in a version where you were the problem, because that's the story your chart reaches for first. Try a different exercise: list what you gave that was good. It is a longer list than you think, and it still counts.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Being left is not a verdict on you. List what you gave. It still counts.

mutual_strong.text: You both ended it, more or less. Mutual endings sound tidy and rarely feel it. With a strong chart you may tell people it was mature and amicable, and maybe it was, but a part of you might still be keeping score of who agreed first. A mutual ending also leaves the door looking open, which invites strong charts to plan the reunion they could engineer. Before you do, remember that you both looked at the same relationship and came to the same conclusion. That's rare. It deserves to be taken seriously, even on the days you'd rather argue with it.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: You both chose this. Don't plan a sequel just because the door looks open.

mutual_weak.text: You both ended it, more or less. For a weak chart, a mutual ending can feel oddly hard to grieve, because nobody is the villain and you don't feel entitled to be sad. You are. Agreeing that something should end doesn't stop it from being a loss. You might also have agreed partly to make it easier for them, and that's worth admitting to yourself. Let yourself be properly sad for a while, without needing a reason that sounds dramatic enough. Quiet losses still deserve attention.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Nobody's the villain, and you're still allowed to be sad. Quiet losses count.

unclear_strong.text: It faded out, or it's complicated. Unclear endings are hard on strong charts because there is nothing to push against. No final conversation, no clear reason, nothing to win or lose. You may be tempted to force a clear ending now, with a big message or a summit. Before you do, check what you want from it. If it's closure, you can give yourself that without them: write down what ended, when you knew, what you'll keep. If it's another round, be honest that this is what the message is for.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: No clear ending? You can write your own. Doesn't need their signature.

unclear_weak.text: It faded out, or it's complicated. For a weak chart, a fade is the hardest kind of ending, because it leaves a question where a door should be. You may still be waiting for the conversation that never happened, or reading every small sign as a maybe. You don't need their participation to call something finished. You can decide it's done for now, for your own peace, and change your mind later if life gives you a reason. Living in the maybe costs too much.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: You can call it finished for your own peace. The maybe is too expensive.

unsaid.text: You didn't say who ended it, and that's fine. However it went, there is usually one person who saw the end first, and one who was told. Both roles hurt. The one who sees it coming grieves early and alone. The one who is told grieves all at once. If you can, figure out which one you were, privately. It changes what you need now. Early grievers often need permission to be done. The ones who were told often need time and a lot of gentleness, including from themselves.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Saw it coming, or got told? Each needs something different. Be honest with yourself.

fresh.text: Less than a month. That's very fresh, and this reading should be read gently. In the first weeks your body is still running the old routines: the good-morning text, the weekend default, the person you would tell about your day. Every one of those habits fires and finds nothing. That is not a sign you should get back together. It is withdrawal, and it fades with time and new routines. Big decisions about them are best left for later. For now, the only job is getting through the evenings.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Under a month is very fresh. The only job right now is getting through the evenings.

months.text: One to six months. This is the stretch where the first shock is gone and the real sorting starts. Friends assume you're fine. Some days you are. Then a song or a street undoes the week. This is also when the pull to check in is strongest, because the pain is quieter and the memories have started to soften. Notice that softening. Memory edits out the hard parts first. Keep one honest note of why it ended and read it when the edited version gets too convincing.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Your memory is a flattering editor. Fact-check it with your own notes.

half.text: Six to twelve months. Long enough that you probably feel you should be over it, short enough that you aren't entirely. That gap can feel embarrassing. It shouldn't. Most people take about this long to stop measuring their days against the relationship. At this stage the question shifts from them to what you've built since. If the honest answer is not much, that's the place to put energy now. A life that's growing makes the past feel smaller without any effort.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Not over it at month eight? Normal. Build something new and the past shrinks on its own.

long.text: Over a year. If you're still reading about this, the relationship left a real mark, and it's worth asking why this one in particular. Often it's not only the person. It's who you were with them, or a version of your future that left with them. Those can be grieved separately. Ask yourself what you miss most, then ask whether it has to come from them. Sometimes the answer is yes. Often it's a part of your own life you can go back and get.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: A year later, ask what you actually miss. Sometimes it's a version of you.

unsaid.text: However long it's been, time is doing two things at once. It is softening the memory, and it is building the habit of thinking about them. The first is natural. The second you can interrupt. When their name shows up in your head, ask a small question back: is this a feeling or a habit? Feelings deserve a minute of attention. Habits deserve a different thought, chosen on purpose.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Feelings get a minute. Habits get a new thought. Learn to tell them apart.

back_strong.text: You said you want to get back together. A strong chart wanting something tends to treat it as a plan, and that's where to be careful. You can't plan another person's heart, and saju can't see theirs. What you can do is make sure the version of you they'd meet is different from the one they left. Spend the next weeks on that, not on them. If a door ever opens, you'll walk through it as someone new. If it doesn't, you'll still have changed in ways that serve every relationship after this one.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Want them back? Work on the you they'd meet. Not on them. Not on strategy.

back_weak.text: You said you want to get back together. With a weak chart, check how much of that want is about them and how much is about the ground falling away when they left. Both are human. But a relationship you return to because you feel unsteady alone tends to repeat the same pattern. Steady yourself first, with sleep, friends and routines, and then see whether the want is still there. If it is, it's a clearer want. If it softens, that tells you something too.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Steady yourself first, then check if you still want them back. Clearer either way.

closure_strong.text: You said you want closure. A strong chart often imagines closure as a final conversation where everything gets said properly. Sometimes that's possible. Often the other person can't give the answer you're looking for, because they don't fully have it. Closure is something you can finish yourself. Write the questions you'd ask, then answer them as honestly as you can from what you know. The answers won't be perfect. They'll be yours, and they won't depend on anyone's schedule.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: You don't need their answers to close this. Write your own. They're usually right.

closure_weak.text: You said you want closure. For a weak chart, closure from them can feel like the only way to feel okay, as if you need their permission to move on. You don't. They might never say the thing you need to hear, and your peace can't wait on that. Try writing a letter you don't send. Say everything, including the unfair parts. Then write one line back to yourself, the kind thing a good friend would say. Read that line on the hard days.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Write the unsendable letter. Then write yourself one kind line back.

move_strong.text: You said you want to stop thinking about them. Strong charts often try to do this by force, and force feeds the thought. The harder you push a memory away, the more it pushes back. Instead, replace. Fill your evenings with things you'd choose anyway. Change one daily route. Delete or archive what you keep rereading. You won't stop thinking about them in a day, but you'll notice the gaps between thoughts getting longer.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Forcing a thought out invites it back in. Replace the habit instead. Boring but works.

move_weak.text: You said you want to stop thinking about them. For a weak chart, intrusive thoughts often show up when you're tired, lonely or overextended. They're a symptom of low reserves as much as feelings. So you'll get further by protecting your energy than by fighting the thoughts directly. Sleep, food, company, and a little less of everything that drains you. As you fill back up, the thoughts get quieter on their own. Be patient with that process.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: The thoughts get loudest when you're tired. Fill up first. They'll get quieter.

unsure_strong.text: You're not sure what you want, which is more honest than it sounds. A strong chart usually wants to decide fast, so not knowing can feel like failing. It isn't. It's the start of a better decision. Give yourself a deadline that isn't tomorrow, maybe a month. Until then, collect evidence: when do you miss them, when are you relieved, which version of the future makes you exhale? At the end, look at the pile. It usually points somewhere.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Not knowing isn't failing. Collect evidence for a month, then look at the pile.

unsure_weak.text: You're not sure what you want, and that's completely okay. For a weak chart, other people's opinions can drown out your own preference, so it's normal to feel foggy. Take a break from asking everyone. Spend a little time alone with the question. Write "I want" and finish the sentence ten times without editing. Some answers will be about them, some won't. The ones that surprise you are usually the most important.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Write "I want" ten times and finish each one. The surprises are the real answer.

jeong-fire.why-it-ended: Jeong Fire is the candle: intimate, focused, the light people sit close to. You love with intensity and pay attention to tiny things, a shift in tone, a reply that came later than usual. That sensitivity makes you a deep partner. It also means you probably noticed the ending long before anyone said it, and maybe you started grieving while you were still in it. Candle types read meaning into small silences and then protect themselves by pulling back first. If this breakup felt like a slow flicker rather than a crash, that's why. Ask yourself honestly: what did I feel early, and did I ever say it out loud?
jeong-fire.your-breakup-pattern: You hold a breakup close. Jeong Fire doesn't announce, it processes, privately and thoroughly, usually around two in the morning. You might analyze every message, reread old notes, build careful theories. You're looking for the meaning, because meaning makes pain bearable. The trap is that thinking about it starts to feel like still being in it. Your other pattern is loyalty to the memory: you keep a little flame lit long after the other person has left the room. That flame is beautiful. It's also yours to set down when your hands get tired.
jeong-fire.the-pull: What pulls you back is intimacy. You let very few people into the small, warm room where your real self lives, and they were in there. Losing that access feels like part of you went dark. Of course you want it back. But the room is still yours. It never belonged to them. Let someone else in, even a little: a friend who's good at deep talks, a sibling, a journal you actually keep. What you need is closeness, and closeness can be rebuilt, slowly, with people who've earned a seat by the candle.
jeong-fire.the-honest-answer: Nobody can tell you what's happening inside someone else's heart, and your chart doesn't hold their choices. It does hold yours. Jeong Fire tends to fixate, letting one person become the whole source of light. If you want them back, ask whether you want them, or the feeling of being deeply known. Ask too whether you felt safe being fully yourself with them, moods included. If the honest answer is mixed, the work isn't winning them back. It's learning to say what you feel while you feel it, so the next ending, if there ever is one, surprises nobody.
jeong-fire.if-they-reach-out: If they reach out, you'll read the message twelve times and decode every comma. Breathe first. Then read it once more as if a friend had sent it to you. What does it actually say? Jeong Fire's intuition is strong, but in heartbreak it can run on fear instead of facts. Reply when you're calm, and not at night. Say one true thing about how you feel, and watch how they handle it. Someone worth reconnecting with can hold your honesty. Someone who flinches from it was probably part of why the light flickered to begin with.
jeong-fire.what-you-do-now: Protect your flame. Jeong Fire burns best in calm rooms, so build some calm. Sleep before midnight when you can. Leave the phone in another room at night. Light an actual candle if you like the ritual. Spend time on something that rewards focus: writing, drawing, slow cooking, learning one deep thing properly. Choose two or three people and tell them more than you usually would. And when the urge to analyze arrives, give it a time limit. Twenty minutes, then close the notebook. You were never only someone's light. You're your own.

jeong-fire.speaker: bom
jeong-fire.text: You noticed everything, Jeong. That's how deeply you loved.

jeong-fire.speaker: yeon
jeong-fire.text: You also saw the ending months early and said nothing. Classic.

jeong-fire.speaker: bom
jeong-fire.text: Your 2am feelings are real, but they're not the whole truth.

jeong-fire.speaker: yeon
jeong-fire.text: Read their message once. Not twelve times. Once.

jeong-fire.speaker: bom
jeong-fire.text: Let a friend into the warm room for a while.

jeong-fire.speaker: yeon
jeong-fire.text: Your flame is yours. Stop handing matches to people who left.

spring.intro: A candle lit in spring has wood stacked all around it. Wood commanded your birth season, Jeong, and Wood feeds Fire, so your inner flame is well supplied with feeling, memory and care. You love with focus: one person, fully seen. That's why this breakup hurts in such detail. You remember the song in the car, the exact wording of that text, the way they said your name. Your fuel is memory itself, and right now you're burning it to keep warm. It works until it doesn't. The spring candle's gift is renewal. You can light from fresh wood: new friends, new rooms, new stories. You don't have to keep burning the old ones.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: You're using old texts as firewood. That supply runs out, Jeong.

summer.intro: A candle in midsummer is a candle in a room full of other flames. Fire held the season you were born in, Jeong, so your chart carries a lot of your own element, which makes you intense, loyal and quietly fierce. In love you probably gave everything to a small circle of two. When it ended, the heat had nowhere to go. You might be burning it as anger, or as hours of analysis, or as a playlist you can't stop replaying. Summer Jeong can mistake intensity for meaning: it hurts this much, so it must be the one. Not necessarily. Sometimes it hurts this much because you're built to burn steadily. Let the flame settle before you read anything into it.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: It hurting this much doesn't make them the one. You just burn hot.

autumn.intro: Autumn Jeong is the candle in the jeweler's workshop, the precise flame that shapes metal. Metal was in command when you were born, and Fire works on Metal, so your love is attentive and crafted. You noticed details, got things just right, remembered something they mentioned once in March. In the relationship you might have spent your flame refining someone who didn't want reshaping, or refining yourself to fit them. The breakup leaves you holding all that careful work. It wasn't wasted. It's a skill, and it belongs to you. The pull back is wanting the craft to have counted. It did. It doesn't need their approval to be real.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: All that care you crafted? Still yours. It goes wherever you go.

winter.intro: A candle in winter matters more than any other light. Water ruled your birth season, Jeong, and Water puts out Fire, so you grew up protecting your flame from drafts. That's why you trust slowly and love deeply once you do. In the relationship you probably cupped your hands around them. After the breakup, the draft got in. You may feel unusually small and flickery right now, and you might be checking their accounts as if hunting for the window that let the cold in. You won't find a full answer there. Winter candles survive inside a lantern: steady people, routines, warm places. Build yours before you go looking for anyone's draft.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Feeling flickery is allowed. Let your people be the lantern for a while.

earth.intro: You came in during the Earth days, Jeong, the weeks when a season winds down and soil takes over. A candle in a clay room: your flame warms the walls, and the walls keep the heat. Fire feeds Earth, so in love you poured attention into making things feel safe and settled. After the breakup, you might replay whether you gave enough. You did. Probably more than enough. The pull back is the comfort you built, not necessarily the person. Keep the comfort. Light it for yourself: your room, your music, your evenings.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: The warm room was your work, Jeong. You get to keep it.

jeong-fire.strong: Your candle has plenty of fuel, Jeong, which makes your love intense, focused and very hard to switch off. You commit with your whole flame. In a breakup that becomes fixation: analyzing, remembering, holding the light up to every detail. You might have pushed for answers they couldn't give. The blind spot is that a steady flame can feel like a spotlight to the person in it. If you're tempted to reach out, check whether you want them or want the story finished. Some stories end mid-sentence. You're allowed to close the book anyway.
jeong-fire.weak: Your flame doesn't get much support in your chart, Jeong, so you protect it carefully and give it away even more carefully. Once you chose them, you probably gave more than you kept. You tended their moods, remembered their needs, apologized first. After the breakup you might feel guttered out, as if you used all your light on someone else. You didn't. A small flame relights easily when it's sheltered. Choose people who cup their hands around you too. Your care is precious. It shouldn't cost you all your warmth.

after-hours.heading: Your after-hours ritual
after-hours.text: The Jeong version of checking is intimate and slow. You don't skim. You reread. One old message thread, one voice note, one photo where the light was perfect. A candle focuses its whole flame on a small circle, and right now the circle is a memory you keep tending. It feels like devotion. It is closer to burning down to the wick on someone who has left the room. Here's a gentler ritual. When the urge comes, light an actual candle and write for the length of time it takes to burn a little. Write what you miss, plainly. Then blow it out and stop. Containing the feeling inside a small ceremony tells your mind it has been honored, and it stops demanding to be honored every hour. Your devotion is precious. Give it a container instead of letting it spill across every night.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Write what you miss while a candle burns. Then blow it out. Feeling honored, tending done.

four-weeks.heading: Your next four weeks
four-weeks.text: Week one: protect your small circle. Spend time with the two or three people who have known you longest, not the wide crowd. Jeong Fire recovers in close quarters. Week two: give your focus to something specific and beautiful. Learn a recipe properly, restore an old piece of furniture, read one author's whole shelf. You need somewhere to put your attention that won't disappoint you. Week three: say one thing you've been holding to the person it belongs to, not the ex, someone else in your life who deserves to hear it. You hold so much in. Week four: notice who has been quietly warming you this whole time. A friend who checks in, a coworker who saves you a seat. Thank them in person. By the end of the month your flame won't be any smaller. It will just be lighting more of the room.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Rereading the same voice note at midnight isn't a ritual, Jeong. It's a loop.

first-message.heading: If they write: your three replies
first-message.text: Your scripts, Jeong, written to keep the flame steady. If you want to talk: "I've thought about you. I'd like to talk, slowly, and see what's there." If you want distance: "Thank you for writing. I care about you, and I need distance to stay okay." If you're unsure: "I'm glad you reached out. I'd like a little time before I reply properly." What to avoid is the all-in reply, the message where your whole heart pours out at once because you've been holding it so long. That much feeling, sent in one go, can scare both of you. Write that version, keep it, and send something shorter. If things go well, there will be time for the rest. Candles last longer when nobody opens the window too fast.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Write the full-heart version and keep it. Send the short one.

gap-wood-and-jeong-fire.title: The oak and the March grudge
gap-wood-and-jeong-fire.you_are_a: Your Jeong Fire ex was the candle by the window: quiet, warm, paying attention to everything. They wrote you long messages after midnight and noticed when your reply was two words shorter than usual. You replied like a train timetable. 'Leaving now.' 'Booked.' To you, reliability was the romance. To them, the missing detail was the whole story. Small hurts piled up somewhere you couldn't see, because you assume silence means fine, and then one evening it all burned at once over something you said in March. You defended yourself. You tried to fix their mood with a plan. They didn't want a plan, they wanted you to sit next to the feeling for a minute. So the ending felt to you like a sudden fire, and to them like a slow dimming you never noticed. What keeps tugging is how tender it was. Nobody else has ever remembered your coffee order and your childhood dog's name. The fix is small: practice the one-detail rule now, with friends. Every message gets one line that proves you heard them. It's awkward for a week. Then it's just who you are.
gap-wood-and-jeong-fire.you_are_b: You loved someone who said 'sounds good' and meant it completely, and somehow that was never quite enough. Your Gap Wood ex was solid, upright, generous in big ways: they showed up, they carried things, they made plans. But they texted like a calendar, and you are someone who reads punctuation like tea leaves. You noticed the shorter replies. You noticed they never asked a follow-up. You didn't say so, because saying it felt needy, so you held it, and held it, until a small thing set the whole stack alight and they stared at you like the fire came from nowhere. To them, it did. Here is the sting: you were hurting in a language they didn't speak, and you never translated. When you were upset, they tried to fix it, which felt like being handled. What pulls you back is the safety. With them, you never once wondered if they'd turn up. One thing to try: write down the three things you never said, plainly, as if to a friend. Not to send. To prove to yourself they were sayable. Then say things like that in the week they happen.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Jeong, they weren't psychic. You needed to say it in March, not October.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Gap, one warm detail per text. That's all the candle needed.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: Two good people, one missing translator.

eul-wood-and-jeong-fire.title: Flowers by candlelight, never said aloud
eul-wood-and-jeong-fire.you_are_a: This one was soft and romantic, and almost nothing important got said out loud. You and your Jeong Fire ex wrote each other long, careful messages and read between every line. You went vague when something hurt. They went quiet. Resentment sat under the candlelight like a draft you could feel but never find. They wanted your attention focused, intensely, on them, and you love a wide circle of friends, so every brunch you went to alone felt to them like a small betrayal and to you like a small cage. You both worried, and together you made the worry bigger: two yin souls whispering the worst-case version to each other at 1am. The hurt here is gentle and long. Nothing exploded. It just got harder to breathe. The intimacy is what you miss. Nobody else listened to your feelings with that much care. Try saying one direct thing, in daylight, to someone you love. Not a hint. Not a meme. 'That upset me.' It feels clumsy. It's also how you stop needing a code to be understood.
